The country palace of the emperor Hadrian below Tivoli, about 20 km from Rome, begun at the end of 118 or early 119 over older villas of the Republic, one perhaps inherited by his wife Vibia Sabina. Hadrian spent much of his reign travelling the empire, and building went on while he was away so that he could come home to finished halls; he made it his official residence around 128 and is believed to have retired here near the end of his life. It covers at least a square kilometre, more than the town of Pompeii, with over 30 large buildings on terraces at different heights among gardens, pools and fountains, fed by the aqueducts that supplied Rome.

Hadrian named parts of it after places he knew, such as the Lyceum and the Academy of Athens. The Poecile, a huge walled garden with a pool 232 m long, copies the Painted Stoa of Athens. The Canopus, named after an Egyptian town on a branch of the Nile, is a long pool lined with statues, among them copies of the maidens of the Erechtheion, ending in a domed outdoor dining hall. The Maritime Theatre is a round retreat 40 m across, an island ringed by a moat and a colonnade, with its own rooms, library and baths. The halls use curved plans in concrete that had no match until the Baroque, and Borromini drew on them. In 1998 archaeologists found the Antinoeion, perhaps a shrine or even the tomb of Antinous, Hadrian's young favourite, in a quarter dressed in Egyptian style.

Later emperors used the villa now and then, and Diocletian restored it, but from the 4th century its statues and marble were carried off, and both sides camped in it during the Gothic War. Rediscovered in the late 15th century, it was stripped again in the 16th by Cardinal Ippolito d'Este for his own villa at Tivoli, and many of its sculptures are now in museums such as the Vatican and the Capitoline. Much of the site is still unexcavated. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999.
